statement: The picture shows shapes 1, 2 and 3 of a pattern made of square tiles. The pattern keeps growing in the same way. How many tiles are in shape 5?

figure.alt: Three T-shapes made of equal square tiles, labelled 1, 2 and 3. Shape 1 has a top row of 3 tiles with 1 tile below the middle, 4 tiles in all. Shape 2 has a top row of 5 tiles with a column of 2 tiles below the middle, 7 tiles in all. Shape 3 has a top row of 7 tiles with a column of 3 tiles below the middle, 10 tiles in all.

choices.misconception: I added only the 1 new tile in the column for each shape after shape 3, so 11 and then 12, and missed that the top row grows too.
I continued the pattern one step too few and found shape 4.
I added only the 2 new tiles in the top row for each shape after shape 3, so 12 and then 14, and missed that the column grows too.
I thought shape 1 has 4 tiles, so shape 5 must have 5 times as many.

hints: Look at the top row and the column separately.
Two things change from one shape to the next. Say in words how the top row changes and how the column changes, then add both changes for each new shape.
Each new shape adds 2 tiles to the top row and 1 tile to the column, so 3 tiles more each time. Shape 3 has 10 tiles.

solutions.reliable: Shape 1 has 4 tiles, shape 2 has 7 and shape 3 has 10: each step adds 2 tiles to the top row and 1 to the column, 3 tiles in all. So shape 4 has 13 tiles and shape 5 has 16. The idea to keep: describe every part that changes before continuing a pattern.
solutions.elegant: Shape 5 has a top row of 11 tiles and a column of 5 tiles below it, so $11 + 5 = 16$.

whyOnTest: A pattern that changes two things at once catches anyone who notices only one of them.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
